Q: Using rsync to remote SSH user with no shell access A:

A 2025 update on the accepted answer. This part is right:

That would probably be the easiest thing to do.

In other words, create a user with a login shell for this purpose.

Using rsync as www-data or similar with SSH key access only is a widely suggested technique. I was shocked to find it no longer works. Of the suggested workarounds:

  • rssh is "done. Period". Ref: https://serverfault.com/q/866102
  • scponly hasn't been touched for 15 years and requires compilation. At least the docs look good, because you're gunna need them!

The up to date suggestion is rush. It installs, but fails mysteriously out of the box (on Ubuntu) and requires intricate configuration (thanks to the author for their documentation efforts).

You might also be tempted to use rrsync, which was designed for this. Despite being more than 20 years old, it seems to have a bit of life. But you have to specify a permitted directory, modify your authorized_keys and install a script file. If you persue this route, this will help.

So in summary, unless you're willing to configure security details on some arguably arcane tools, I suggest you create a limited access user, disable their password, give them group permissions to your site files, and control who has the private key.

Q: Launch suprocesses in Python by chunks and wait until end for start the next chunk A:

While arguably a little wasteful, that's a huge benefit of Python: ease of development for a slower runtime

Consider instead of waiting for each chunk, a design where you

  • create a collection of tasks
  • start a thread for each parallel job
    • which consume the tasks
    • manages the subprocess
  • join all the tasks

I also highly recommend checking the result of each process and retrying or failing early if they're not completing - in this design, you can even recreate failed jobs right away by just adding it back to the queue, but I'd do this sparingly and track either individually (job contains a counter for errors) or totally (global counter or length of a collection of failed jobs, which can contain their stderr, etc.) how many failed jobs you have for your attempts or entire process to end early

from collections import deque  # friendly API, or consider queue.SimpleQueue
from subprocess import Popen, PIPE
from threading import Thread

def worker(Q_jobs, Q_results):
    while True:
        job = Q_jobs.pop()
        if job is None: break  # one of many exit designs
        name, command = job
        p = Popen(command, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)
        out, err = p.communicate()  # wait for completion and get the results
        Q_results.append((name, p.returncode))  # track results

def main():
    Q_jobs, Q_results = deque(), deque()
    count = 9  # set from cores or arg
    #<fill Q_jobs with tasks here>

    workers = []
    for index in range(count):
        t = Thread(worker, args=(Q_jobs, Q_results))
        Q_jobs.append(None)  # end each Thread
    for t in workers:
        t.start()
    # work has now started, opportunity to monitor progress too

    # wait for worker to exit
    for t in workers:
        t.join()

    # check the results

Q: Why do integration tests remove IDbContextOptionsConfiguration<TContext> instead of the DbContext itself A:

That happens due to the internal workings of the EF Core registration - it registers IDbContextOptionsConfiguration somewhere along the standard DI proccess (source). Since the registration is "absolute" when you reregister context with another database provider it results in multiple providers configured exception (source, example) due to extra check.

No such thing happens for DB context because multiple registration override each other, i.e. only the last one will be used by default and basically the main thing you need to override is the options for the context which will be resolved on context construction, not the context itself.

Q: How should @version be used in phpDoc? A:

You are correct in "the @version can be used multiple times in a project". The tag is deliberately flexible, and can be used from one extreme (the version of the overall package, so all tags show the same value) to the other extreme (every single class/method/function/whatever has its own version # and change history, so a class at v1.2.3 could have ten methods all showing their own different version numbers). In general, however, I don't believe I've ever seen a case where the version was used any more granularly than at the "installable library/package/application level".

Regarding the @since tag... in whatever style you use the @version tag for a given element, the @since tag represents the version # that the element was first introduced. A variation on this is where you use the @since tag like a changelog, and thus you have multiple @since tags on the same element (see the dump() function example here -- https://docs.phpdoc.org/guide/references/phpdoc/tags/since.html).

My suggestion in how to use these tags:

  • the 'version' is the overall release version of a package/library/application as denoted by all of it being in one version control repository
  • I would only put @version tags in file-level docblocks, class-level docblocks, and standalone function docblocks
  • I would only use @since tags on API-level classes and methods

It would be easy to overuse these tags, and thus make maintenance of the values of the tags a nightmare.

Q: ArgoCD helm chart how to override values yml in declarative helm chart deployment App/controller A:

Looks like,

The helm chart in the artifactory has a key : value combination say

# value present in the helm chart values.yaml 
app-details: 
   name: "demoapp"
   version: "1.0"
   description: "simple demo app"

In argoCd application manifest

# .....
  helm:
       releaseName: <release-name-hardcoded>
       # custom values to override the helm chart one
       values: |
          app-details : 
             name: "demoapp"
             version: "1.0"
             # if I didn't specify the description here <--------------- *
# ....

* - ArgoCd is setting the default value (from values.yaml) for description key in this case. This description value can be seen in the deployed manifest.

Also the values.yml data are displayed as parameter in the UI.

I had to use a different approach, where I need to make changes in the template charts that uses this description value.
